about.title: Rolling Hills Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Rolling Hills is a small, quiet community of under 2,000 residents, but that doesn't mean workplace injuries don't happen here. Landscaping crews, private household staff, security personnel, contractors working on the winding roads near Crenshaw Boulevard or Crest Road West, and delivery drivers navigating Silver Spur Road all face real on-the-job risks. In California, workers' compensation is generally the only path against your employer, but it doesn't tell the whole story. If a subcontractor, equipment manufacturer, property owner, or another driver contributed to your injury, you may have a separate claim worth exploring. Our team reviews both the workers' comp side and any third-party angle for injured workers in Rolling Hills, free of charge, so you understand where you actually stand before making decisions about your case.

whyChoose.title: Why Rolling Hills Workers Choose Us

items.title: Understanding What Workers' Comp Covers
items.desc: California generally treats workers' comp as the exclusive remedy against your employer regardless of fault. We can help you understand whether that applies fully to your situation.

items.title: Spotting Third-Party Responsibility
items.desc: If a subcontractor, property owner, equipment maker, or another driver contributed to your injury, a separate claim may be possible outside the workers' comp system. Third-party claims in California carry a 2-year filing deadline.

items.title: Protection Against Retaliation
items.desc: Reporting a workplace injury to your employer within 30 days is required, and California law makes it illegal for an employer to retaliate against you for doing so. Knowing your rights early can matter.

items.question: I was hurt working on a private property in Rolling Hills. Do I only have a workers' comp claim?
items.answer: Not necessarily. Workers' comp is usually the exclusive remedy against your direct employer, but if a separate contractor, equipment supplier, or another party's negligence played a role, you may have an additional claim. We can review the specifics of your situation and tell you what applies.

items.question: How soon do I need to report my injury to my employer?
items.answer: California law requires you to report a workplace injury to your employer within 30 days. Missing that window can complicate your claim, so it's best to report as soon as possible after the incident.

items.question: Can my employer punish me for filing a workplace injury claim?
items.answer: No. Retaliation against an employee for reporting a workplace injury or filing a claim is illegal under California law. If you believe you've faced retaliation, that's something we can help you address alongside your injury claim.
